title: EUR 500,000 on four rails, four views, one customer asking where it is
explain:
A bank runs EUR 500,000 a day across four rails.
Domestic, cross-border, real-time and high-value each have their own view.
A customer asks where a payment is.
Four teams give four answers.

Here is how that happens:

→ Domestic payment, one platform view
→ Cross-border payment, another view
→ Real-time payment, a third view
→ High-value payment, a fourth view
→ Same customer, same question, four different answers

The assumption was:
"Each rail needs its own platform and its own controls."

GPP orchestrates multiple payment types and rails from one platform: domestic, cross-border, real-time and high-value payments, with routing, compliance and reconciliation.

Why?

One platform means one set of controls and one view of the payment, whatever the rail. Separate platforms give each rail its own truth, and the customer hears all four at once.

One platform, one view, whatever the rail.

Why do four teams give four answers about one payment?

BA Takeaway

Run every rail on one platform, with one set of controls and one view.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic payments, on the one platform
→ Cross-border payments, on the one platform
→ Real-time payments, on the one platform
→ High-value payments, on the one platform
→ Routing, compliance and reconciliation, one set of controls

Show the payment once, with its rail labelled, never once per rail system.

The real requirement is not "Which rail was it?"

It is "What evidence proves one platform saw the whole payment?"

Have you heard four answers about one payment?
takeaway: One platform means one set of controls and one view of the payment, whatever the rail.

title: EUR 750,000 cross-border payment, the weakest hand-off breaks it
explain:
A EUR 750,000 cross-border payment crosses seven hand-offs.
Six are strong. One is weak.
The payment fails at the weak one.
The integration was judged by its best hand-off.

Here is how that happens:

→ Initiation, payment starts in the channel
→ Validation and enrichment, checked and enriched
→ Compliance, checked before routing
→ Routing and orchestration, routed across rails from one platform
→ ISO 20022 and SWIFT, mapped and sent
→ Exceptions, handled when a stage fails
→ Settlement and reconciliation, settled, then reconciled

The assumption was:
"Most hand-offs strong means the integration is strong."

GPP integration in cross-border payments covers initiation, validation and enrichment, compliance, routing and orchestration, ISO 20022 and SWIFT, exceptions, and settlement with reconciliation.

Why?

Each stage is a hand-off, and the integration is only as strong as the weakest hand-off. A chain judged by its strongest link hides the one that breaks, and the payment finds it.

Strongest link thinking breaks chains.

Why does a payment with six strong hand-offs fail?

BA Takeaway

Test the weakest hand-off first, and strengthen it before praising the rest.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiation and validation, where the payment is prepared
→ Compliance and routing, where it is cleared and sent
→ ISO 20022 and SWIFT, where it is mapped and carried
→ Exceptions, where a stage failure is handled
→ Settlement and reconciliation, where it closes

Score every hand-off, and report the weakest score as the integration score.

The real requirement is not "How strong is the integration?"

It is "What evidence proves the weakest hand-off holds?"

Have you seen a chain break at its weakest hand-off?
takeaway: Each stage is a hand-off, and the integration is only as strong as the weakest hand-off.

title: EUR 900,000 payment works, the lending product beside it breaks
explain:
A BA fixes a EUR 900,000 payment flow.
The payment works.
A lending product that shares the same platform breaks the same week.
The BA never looked beyond payments.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment flow fixed, tested, working
→ Wider platform untouched, never reviewed
→ Lending product shares platform services
→ Change in payments breaks lending, no one saw the link

The assumption was:
"Payments is the whole platform."

The banking technology platform is a banking ecosystem, broader than a payment processor alone.

Why?

Its products cover more of the bank than payments, so a BA working with the platform must understand the wider platform, not only the payment flow. A change that is safe inside payments can break a product that shares its services, and the BA who never looked wider never sees the link.

Payments is one part of the platform.

Why does a safe payments change break lending?

BA Takeaway

Map the wider platform before changing any part of it, and check every shared service.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payments, one part of the wider platform
→ Wider banking products, covering more of the bank than payments
→ Shared services, where a change in one product touches another
→ The BA view, the whole platform, not only payments

List the products that share each service before any change ships.

The real requirement is not "Does the payment work?"

It is "What evidence proves no wider product broke when the payment changed?"

takeaway: Its products cover more of the bank than payments, so a BA must understand the wider platform, not only the payment flow.

title: EUR 1,200,000 a day, channels connected, hub never reached
explain:
A bank connects its channels and systems to the payment hub.
EUR 1,200,000 a day should flow end to end.
It does not.
The plumbing was connected, but the nine-step journey was never tested through it.

Here is how that happens:

→ Channels and systems connected to the hub
→ Payment enters the channel
→ Hub receives it, journey should run end to end
→ One hand-off in the middle was never wired, journey stalls

The assumption was:
"Connecting the systems is the same as connecting the journey."

Integration connects the bank's channels and systems to the payment hub so that a payment can flow end to end.

Why?

The integration is the plumbing that makes the nine-step journey possible, but plumbing alone is not a journey. A connection that was never tested end to end leaves a hand-off unwired, and the payment stalls in the middle of a flow everyone believed was connected.

Connected systems, disconnected journey.

Why does EUR 1,200,000 a day stall in a fully connected bank?

BA Takeaway

Test the journey, not the connections, and prove every hand-off carries a payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channels and systems, connected to the hub
→ Payment hub, where payments flow end to end
→ Nine-step journey, made possible by the integration
→ End-to-end proof, a payment through every hand-off

Run a payment through all nine steps after every integration change, and show the proof.

The real requirement is not "Are the systems connected?"

It is "What evidence proves a payment flows end to end through the integration?"

Have you seen connected systems with a disconnected journey?
takeaway: The integration is the plumbing that makes the nine-step journey possible.

title: Treasury saw EUR 18 million and thought EUR 2 million was lost
explain:
Treasury expects EUR 20 million.

The advice shows EUR 18 million.

The missing EUR 2 million is not lost. It is still in transit.

Here is how it happens:

→ pacs.009 ADV arrives
→ Treasury reads EUR 18 million
→ The missing EUR 2 million is treated as lost
→ pacs.008, the payment itself, has not arrived yet

The assumption was:
"The advice is the payment."

Why?

A pacs.009 ADV is an advice that funds are on the way, giving treasury visibility before arrival for liquidity planning and forecasting. It is not a pacs.008 payment instruction, and it may carry only part of the amount.

An advice is not a payment.

BA Takeaway

Read the advice and the payment apart. Treasury must know what has arrived, what is advised, and what is still in transit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Advice amount in pacs.009 ADV
→ Payment amount in pacs.008
→ Funds still in transit

The real requirement is not "How much does the advice show?"

It is "What evidence proves how much has actually arrived?"

Have you seen an advice mistaken for the payment itself?
takeaway: An advice is not a payment. pacs.009 ADV gives treasury sight, it does not move money.

title: The team asked for pacs.009 and got the wrong one
explain:
A EUR 100,000 cover payment needs to move.

The requirement says one word: pacs.009.

The team builds Core. The payment needs Cover. The funding leg never moves.

Here is how it happens:

→ Requirement says pacs.009 is needed
→ No use case is named
→ Team builds Core, a bank-to-bank transfer
→ The business needed COV, the cover leg
→ The cover cannot settle, and the customer payment stalls

The assumption was:
"pacs.009 is the requirement."

Why?

COV and ADV are not separate messages in the ISO 20022 catalogue. They share one underlying pacs.009 message, applied to a different business use case. CBPR+ sets out Core, Cover and Advise for cross-border payments, while the EPC SEPA schemes do not use pacs.009 at all.

A message name is not a use case.

BA Takeaway

A requirement that says only that pacs.009 is needed stays incomplete until it also names the use case, the scheme, the usage guideline and the business context.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message name
→ Business use case
→ Scheme and usage guideline

The real requirement is not "Which message do we need?"

It is "What evidence proves the use case, not just the message name?"

Have you seen a build go wrong because the requirement named a message but never named the use case?
takeaway: A message name is not a use case. Name the use case, the scheme and the business context.

title: The team heard MT was dead, and stopped planning for it
explain:
The CBPR+ November 2026 deadline is announced as the end of MT for cross-border payments.

The team stops planning for MT altogether.

Then a EUR 500,000 payment type that still runs on MT after the deadline breaks, because nobody planned for it.

Here is how it happens:

→ November 2026 deadline is announced
→ Team reads it as the end of all MT
→ Many MT messages do migrate to MX by then
→ Some were already retired, and others keep running after the deadline for specialised or domestic use
→ A payment type still on MT is left without a plan

The assumption was:
"MT ends in November 2026."

Why?

SWIFT is driving the migration because MT cannot carry the rich data, structured addresses and granularity that compliance and monitoring need. But the end date is not the same for every message, and that nuance matters in migration planning.

MT is retiring, not retired.

BA Takeaway

Know the nuance rather than repeating the slogan. Plan per message, not per deadline.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message inventory
→ Migration date per message
→ Specialised and domestic use that continues

The real requirement is not "When does MT end?"

It is "What evidence proves which messages migrate, and when?"

Have you seen a migration plan break because the deadline was treated as one date for every message?
takeaway: MT is retiring, not retired. The end date is not the same for every message.

title: The MT103 that lost its address in translation
explain:
An MT103 arrives for a EUR 60,000 payment.

The address is free text, four lines of 35 characters.

In MX it must be structured: name, town, country. The mapping drops the town, and Compliance holds the payment.

Here is how it happens:

→ MT103 arrives with a free-text address
→ Translator converts field by field to MX
→ Town and country are not carried across
→ MX arrives with an incomplete structured address
→ Compliance holds the EUR 60,000 payment

The assumption was:
"Conversion is a format change."

Why?

MT messages are FIN messages written as structured text with character limits, while MX messages are ISO 20022 XML with properly structured data. The translator must also look at the MT structure, correspondent and account information and the business rules to derive the right MX settlement method.

MT to MX is a business mapping exercise, not a format change.

BA Takeaway

Get the mapping right early, because that is what keeps straight-through processing high. Test the mapping with real addresses, not clean samples.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT structure and limits
→ MX structured data
→ Settlement method derivation

The real requirement is not "Did the format change?"

It is "What evidence proves every MT field lands in the right MX element?"

Have you seen a payment held because a field was lost in MT to MX translation?
takeaway: MT to MX is a business mapping exercise, not a format change. Get the mapping right early.

title: The Rs. 4,500 card payment that cleared but never settled
explain:
A customer pays Rs. 4,500 by card.

Authorisation is approved. Clearing completes.

Settlement breaks, and the ledger does not agree. The customer thinks the payment worked. The money is unaccounted for.

Here is how it happens:

→ Authorisation: issuer approves the payment at the point of sale
→ Clearing: network exchanges records between acquirer and issuer
→ Settlement: funds should move between the banks
→ Reconciliation: clearing records, settlement positions and ledger postings do not agree

The assumption was:
"Authorisation means the money moved."

Why?

A card transaction moves through four stages across four parties, and a failure at any stage has a different owner and a different fix. The issuer, the acquirer, the network and the merchant each play a distinct role at each stage.

Know the stage, and you know who must act.

BA Takeaway

Check each stage in order. Authorisation, clearing, settlement and reconciliation are separate controls, and each needs its own evidence.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Authorisation
→ Clearing
→ Settlement
→ Reconciliation

The real requirement is not "Was the payment approved?"

It is "What evidence proves each stage completed, not just the first?"

Have you seen a payment that looked successful at the till, and failed three stages later?
takeaway: Know the stage, and you know who must act. Authorisation is not settlement.

title: Same terminal, same Rs. 10,000, two different kinds of money
explain:
Two customers each pay Rs. 10,000 at the same terminal.

One pays by debit card, one by credit card.

The terminal experience looks identical. The money movement is entirely different.

Here is how it happens:

→ Debit card: payment draws directly on the customer balance
→ Funds leave the account at authorisation
→ Credit card: payment draws on a credit line
→ Issuer funds the payment, and the customer repays later
→ Settlement timing, interest treatment and issuer risk all differ

The assumption was:
"A card payment is a card payment."

Why?

A debit card moves money the customer already holds, while a credit card moves money the issuer lends. The terminal hides the difference, and the ledger does not.

The terminal looks identical. The money movement is not.

BA Takeaway

Always ask which funding source a payment uses, because it decides settlement timing, interest and risk.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Funding source
→ Settlement timing
→ Issuer risk

The real requirement is not "Was the card accepted?"

It is "What evidence proves which funding source this payment used?"

Have you seen a card flow designed as if debit and credit were the same thing?
takeaway: The terminal looks identical, but the account and settlement implications are entirely different.

title: The Rs. 40 lakh payment sent on the wrong rail
explain:
A customer needs Rs. 40 lakh to reach a supplier today.

The payment goes by NEFT, in a batch, because that is the usual rail.

It arrives in the next cycle. The supplier is not paid today, and the customer is furious.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment is urgent and high value
→ NEFT is chosen by habit
→ NEFT settles in batches, and the payment waits
→ RTGS would have settled it individually in central bank money
→ IMPS would have settled it instantly, around the clock

The assumption was:
"Use the usual rail."

Why?

NEFT, RTGS and IMPS are three domestic rails with different operating models. Compare them on speed, availability, settlement model and customer use case, and use the current scheme rules rather than an old summary.

The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit.

BA Takeaway

Route by need: batch and can wait, individual and final, or instant and around the clock. Check the current scheme rules before choosing.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Speed the payment needs
→ Availability the payment needs
→ Settlement model that fits

The real requirement is not "Which rail do we usually use?"

It is "What evidence proves the rail matches the payment's need?"

Have you seen an urgent payment miss its day because it went on the wrong rail?
takeaway: The rail is chosen by the payment's need, not by habit.

title: The Rs. 30 lakh loan that stalled between approval and money
explain:
A customer is approved for a Rs. 30 lakh loan.

The money does not arrive.

Nobody can say where it stopped, because the failure sits at a later stage than the approval.

Here is how it happens:

→ Application collects the request and supporting information
→ Decision assesses credit and affordability
→ Agreement records the terms
→ Disbursement should release the funds
→ Servicing collects repayments and manages changes
→ Closure confirms the balance is settled
→ A weak link at one stage shows up downstream

The assumption was:
"Approval means the money is on its way."

Why?

Each stage has its own data, controls and hand-offs, so a failure at one stage does not always show up until a later stage.

A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream.

BA Takeaway

Trace the chain stage by stage. Do not assume the approval was the problem.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Decision and agreement
→ Disbursement
→ Servicing and closure

The real requirement is not "Was the loan approved?"

It is "What evidence proves every stage handed off cleanly?"

Have you seen a loan stall between approval and disbursement, with nobody able to say where it stopped?
takeaway: A loan is a chain, and a weak link anywhere shows up downstream.

title: Tomorrow, the customer was told, and the money came in two days
explain:
A customer sends Rs. 2 lakh and is told the money will arrive tomorrow.

It arrives in two days.

The complaint was avoidable. The timing quoted was never the scheme's timing.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment is made
→ Customer is told it arrives tomorrow
→ Scheme settles in two days for this product
→ Customer waits, then complains

The assumption was:
"T+1 is the timing."

Why?

A settlement cycle is the period after which funds move between banks, and T+1 or T+2 are only examples of how long that can take. The actual timing depends on the scheme and the product.

Tell the customer the real timing for that product.

BA Takeaway

Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, because telling a customer the money will arrive tomorrow when the scheme settles in two days creates a complaint that was avoidable.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme rule
→ Product rule
→ Customer message

The real requirement is not "What is the usual timing?"

It is "What evidence proves the timing we quoted matches the scheme rule?"

Have you seen a complaint created by a timing promise the scheme could never keep?
takeaway: Customer communication must state the real timing for that product, not a generic T+1.

title: The EUR 20,000 payment that could be taken but never refunded
explain:
A customer pays EUR 20,000 through a new checkout.

The payment goes through. Then the customer asks for a refund.

There is no refund API. There is no reversal API. The money is stuck.

Here is how it happens:

→ Checkout API initiates the payment
→ Authentication API proves who is paying
→ Status API reports where the payment stands
→ Refund API does not exist
→ Reversal API does not exist
→ A payment that can be taken cannot be refunded or checked

The assumption was:
"Build the payment API first."

Why?

A payment product exposes several APIs across the lifecycle, not just one for taking payment. Map each touchpoint to the lifecycle stage it serves, or the product ends up with a payment that can be taken but cannot be refunded or checked.

Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete.

BA Takeaway

Cover initiate, authenticate, check status, refund and reverse before launch. A missing lifecycle stage is a customer problem, not a backlog item.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Initiate and authenticate
→ Status
→ Refund and reversal

The real requirement is not "Can we take the payment?"

It is "What evidence proves every lifecycle stage has an API?"

Have you seen a product that could take money but had no way to give it back?
takeaway: Coverage of the whole lifecycle is what makes a payment product complete.

title: Refund or reversal: the Rs. 8,000 that was posted twice
explain:
A Rs. 8,000 payment should never have completed.

The team issues a refund.

A new credit posts to the customer, while the original posting still stands. The customer is credited twice.

Here is how it happens:

→ Payment should not have completed
→ Team calls it a refund
→ Refund posts as a new credit to the customer
→ Original posting is never unwound
→ Customer is credited twice

The assumption was:
"Refund and reversal are the same thing."

Why?

A refund returns money for a completed payment and posts as a new credit, while a reversal cancels a payment that should not have completed and unwinds the original posting. Validate the rail and provider semantics before building either one, because the same word can mean different things on different rails.

Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow.

BA Takeaway

Decide the ledger effect before the name. A refund creates a credit, a reversal unwinds the posting.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Trigger for the action
→ Timing of the action
→ Ledger effect

The real requirement is not "What do we call it?"

It is "What evidence proves the ledger effect matches the word we used?"

Have you seen a refund and a reversal confused, and the ledger pay for it?
takeaway: Build the ledger effect first, and the name will follow. A refund creates a credit, a reversal unwinds the posting.

title: The Rs. 50,000 payment failed, and three parties pointed at each other
explain:
A Rs. 50,000 card payment fails.

The gateway says it is the bank. The bank says it is the merchant. The merchant says it is the gateway.

The customer waits while three parties argue about ownership.

Here is how it happens:

→ Gateway orchestrates the instruction
→ Bank authorises and processes the payment
→ Merchant is notified of the outcome
→ Payment fails
→ Nobody owns the fix, and nobody tells the customer

The assumption was:
"Someone will handle the failure."

Why?

The gateway, the bank and the merchant each own a distinct part. When a payment fails, knowing which party owns which step decides who must fix it and who must tell the customer.

Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties.

BA Takeaway

Make the boundary between gateway, bank and merchant explicit in the design, for the happy path and for every failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Gateway ownership
→ Bank ownership
→ Merchant ownership

The real requirement is not "Who built this step?"

It is "What evidence proves who owns each step when it fails?"

Have you seen a failed payment turn into a dispute because nobody owned the step that broke?
takeaway: Unclear ownership turns every failure into a dispute between parties.

title: EUR 90,000 cover, and two different ordering customers
explain:
A EUR 90,000 cover payment arrived.
The MT103 named one ordering customer.
The MT202 COV named a different one.
The operations team spent a day arguing over who had sent the payment.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 names the instructing customer
→ MT202 COV names the funding bank
→ Team treats them as one party
→ Screening and reporting land on the wrong party

The assumption was:
"One payment, one ordering customer."
Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg.

Why?

The MT103 names the customer who instructed the payment, while the MT202 COV names the bank moving the funds. Treating them as one party confuses the screening, the reporting and the audit trail.

Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg.

What proves which party counts for which leg?

BA Takeaway

Read the ordering party per message, per leg. Screen the MT103 party as the instructing customer and the MT202 COV party as the funding bank, and never merge the two.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Ordering party on the MT103
→ Ordering party on the MT202 COV
→ Screening per leg

The real requirement isn't "Who sent this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves which party counts for which leg?"

Have you ever seen two messages name two different ordering customers?
takeaway: Each message has its own ordering party for its own leg.

title: EUR 75,000 cover, and field 72 sent the funds to the wrong place
explain:
A EUR 75,000 cover payment was sent with a free-text instruction in field 72.
The next bank read it the wrong way.
The funds went to the wrong place, and settlement stopped.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT202 COV sent with field 72 filled
→ Instruction written loosely, in free text
→ Next bank acts on the wrong reading
→ Funds sent astray, settlement delayed

The assumption was:
"Field 72 is free text, so any wording will do."
Free text is exactly why discipline matters.

Why?

Field 72 carries sender-to-receiver information, and in a cover payment it tells the next bank what the cover is for and what to do with it. A wrong instruction can send the funds to the wrong place or delay settlement.

Put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects.

What proves the next bank will read this instruction the way we meant it?

BA Takeaway

Put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects. Nothing extra, nothing vague. Check the wording against what the receiving bank expects before sending.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction the next bank needs
→ Form the next bank expects
→ Nothing extra, nothing vague

The real requirement isn't "Was field 72 filled in?"

It's "What evidence proves the next bank will read this instruction the way we meant it?"

Have you ever seen a free-text field send funds astray?
takeaway: Put only the instruction the next bank needs, in the form the next bank expects.

title: USD 100,000 sent, USD 99,850 received, and no one could explain the gap
explain:
A customer sent USD 100,000 by serial payment.
The beneficiary was credited USD 99,850.
USD 150 had vanished, and no one at the bank could explain where it went.

Here's how that happens:

→ Ordering customer sends USD 100,000
→ First intermediary deducts its charge
→ Second intermediary deducts its charge
→ Beneficiary credited USD 99,850

The assumption was:
"The beneficiary receives what the sender sent."
In a serial payment, every intermediary deducts its own charge on the way.

Why?

The ordering customer bears the charges, and each intermediary bank deducts its own charge from the amount as the payment passes through. The beneficiary therefore receives the amount minus the charges deducted at each step.

In a serial payment, every deduction in the chain lands on the beneficiary.

What proves each deduction in the chain was agreed and expected?

BA Takeaway

Price a serial payment by accounting for every deduction in the chain, not just the first one. Show the customer the expected credit before sending, and reconcile the actual credit against every charge taken.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Amount sent
→ Each intermediary charge
→ Final credit
→ Customer told the expected credit

The real requirement isn't "Did the beneficiary get the full amount?"

It's "What evidence proves each deduction in the chain was agreed and expected?"

Have you ever had to explain a short credit to a customer who expected the full amount?
takeaway: In a serial payment, every deduction in the chain lands on the beneficiary.

title: USD 100,000, and the charges were counted twice
explain:
A USD 100,000 payment mixed serial and cover legs.
Charges were deducted on the serial leg, then charged again on the cover leg.
The beneficiary was short, and the customer was charged twice for the same journey.

Here's how that happens:

→ Serial leg deducts charges step by step
→ Cover leg handles its charges separately
→ Payment mixes the two methods
→ Beneficiary short, customer double-charged

The assumption was:
"Charges work the same way in every payment."
Charge arithmetic follows the payment method.

Why?

In a serial payment charges are deducted step by step as the payment passes through each intermediary, while in a cover payment the charges on the information leg and the funds leg are handled separately. A payment that mixes the two methods without care can double-charge or under-charge.

Know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive.

What proves the charges were counted once, under the right method?

BA Takeaway

Identify the method first, serial or cover, then apply its charge arithmetic. Never mix the two without working out where each charge lands.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payment method
→ Charges on the serial leg
→ Charges on the cover leg
→ Final credit

The real requirement isn't "Were the charges calculated correctly?"

It's "What evidence proves the charges were counted once, under the right method?"

Have you ever found a payment where the charges were counted twice?
takeaway: Know which method applies before working out what the beneficiary will receive.

title: EUR 25,000 stuck, and the team sent a camt.056 when they needed a camt.026
explain:
EUR 25,000 could not be applied by the receiving bank.
The team sent a camt.056 to recall it.
Nothing happened, because a recall asks for money back, and this payment needed a report that it could not be applied.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment cannot be applied
→ Team sends camt.056 recall
→ No funds to recall, nothing happens
→ Correct message, camt.026, never sent

The assumption was:
"Both messages are about a payment that did not complete, so either will do."
They do different jobs.

Why?

A camt.056 requests a recall of a payment, asking the beneficiary bank to return funds that have already been credited. A camt.026 reports that a payment cannot be applied, telling the sender that the instruction could not be processed.

One asks for money back. The other reports it could not be applied.

What proves we sent the message that matches what actually happened?

BA Takeaway

Ask first what happened: were funds credited and need returning, or could the instruction not be applied at all? Send camt.056 for the first, camt.026 for the second, and never swap them.

Keep these controls separate:

→ What actually happened
→ Funds credited or not
→ Message that matches

The real requirement isn't "Which message do we send?"

It's "What evidence proves we sent the message that matches what actually happened?"

Have you ever sent the wrong message for a payment that could not be applied?
takeaway: One asks for money back. The other reports it could not be applied.

title: EUR 65,000 MT103 arrived with field 57 empty
explain:
An MT103 for EUR 65,000 arrived with field 57 empty.
It named no beneficiary bank.
The receiving bank held it, unsure whether the payment was broken or meant to be handled in house.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 arrives with field 57 empty
→ No beneficiary bank named
→ Receiving bank works out the route from the other fields
→ Payment held while the team decides

The assumption was:
"An empty field is an error."
The empty field is not necessarily an error.

Why?

An empty field 57 can mean the payment is to be handled by the receiving bank itself, or that the beneficiary bank is identified elsewhere in the chain. The analyst must read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission.

Read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission.

What proves this empty field is deliberate, not a gap?

BA Takeaway

Read the whole MT103 before judging field 57. Check the other fields for the beneficiary bank, and only raise an exception when the message as a whole names no route.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Whole message read
→ Beneficiary bank found elsewhere or not
→ Route decided on the full message

The real requirement isn't "Is field 57 empty?"

It's "What evidence proves this empty field is deliberate, not a gap?"

Have you ever held a payment over an empty field that turned out to be deliberate?
takeaway: Read the whole message before deciding whether the empty field is a gap or a deliberate omission.

title: Parent paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries, and the screening landed on the wrong party
explain:
A parent company paid EUR 300,000 for three subsidiaries with one MT101.
The bank reported all three payments under the parent.
Screening and accounting landed on the wrong party for every one of them.

Here's how that happens:

→ Parent instructs with an MT101
→ General instruction sequence carried
→ Subsidiary named per transaction
→ Bank reports under the parent, not the subsidiary

The assumption was:
"The sender is the party that matters."
The subsidiary is the ordering customer for its own transaction.

Why?

The MT101 carries a general instruction sequence and a per-transaction sequence, and the subsidiary appears as the ordering customer in the per-transaction sequence. The parent's bank must then report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party.

Report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party.

What proves each transaction was reported under the right subsidiary?

BA Takeaway

Name the subsidiary as the ordering customer in the per-transaction sequence. Report, screen and account for each transaction under that subsidiary, not under the parent.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Ordering customer per transaction
→ Reporting per subsidiary
→ Screening per subsidiary

The real requirement isn't "Who sent this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves each transaction was reported under the right subsidiary?"

Have you ever seen a group payment reported under the wrong company?
takeaway: Report each transaction under the correct subsidiary, so the accounting and the screening both land on the right party.

title: EUR 120,000 credited twice because a notification was sent as an MT103
explain:
EUR 120,000 was credited to a customer.
The bank then sent an MT103 to report the credit.
The receiving bank read it as an instruction to pay, and debited the account a second time.

Here's how that happens:

→ Credit already made to the customer
→ Bank sends an MT103 to report it
→ Receiving bank reads it as an instruction to pay
→ Account debited a second time

The assumption was:
"An MT103 can report a credit."
An MT103 instructs a payment. It is not a notification.

Why?

An MT103 instructs the receiving bank to debit the sender's account and pay the beneficiary, so it is an instruction to move money. When a bank only wants to say that an account has already been credited, it uses an MT910 confirmation of credit or an MT950 or MT940 statement instead.

An instruction is not a notification. Sending one as the other moves money twice.

What proves this message instructs a payment, rather than reporting one?

BA Takeaway

Use an MT103 only to instruct a payment. Report a credit already made with an MT910, an MT950 or an MT940, and never send an instruction where a notification belongs.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Message purpose
→ Instruction or notification
→ Correct message chosen

The real requirement isn't "Was the credit reported?"

It's "What evidence proves this message instructs a payment, rather than reporting one?"

Have you ever seen a notification move money because it used the wrong message?
takeaway: An instruction is not a notification. Sending one as the other moves money twice.

title: USD 75,000 MT103, and the intermediary was named in the wrong field
explain:
A USD 75,000 MT103 travelled through an intermediary bank.
The intermediary was named in field 55 instead of field 56.
The funds went for reimbursement through a bank that was never meant to handle them.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 names the intermediary in field 55
→ Field 56 left empty
→ Funds routed as a reimbursement, not a forward
→ Payment goes astray

The assumption was:
"Fields 55 and 56 both name banks in the middle, so either will do."
Field 56 names the intermediary. Field 55 names a third reimbursement institution.

Why?

Field 56 names the intermediary institution, the bank that receives the payment from the sender and forwards it to the account with institution in field 57. Field 55 names a third reimbursement institution, used when the funds are reimbursed through a bank that is neither the sender nor the receiver.

Field 56 names the intermediary. Field 55 names the reimbursement bank. Swap them and the funds go astray.

What proves the intermediary is named in field 56, not field 55?

BA Takeaway

Put the intermediary in field 56A when a serial chain gains an intermediary. Use field 55 only for a third reimbursement institution, and leave field 56 out entirely when the receiver is its own correspondent.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 56 intermediary
→ Field 55 reimbursement
→ Field 57 account with institution

The real requirement isn't "Is a bank named in the middle?"

It's "What evidence proves the intermediary is named in field 56, not field 55?"

Have you ever seen fields 55 and 56 swapped on an MT103?
takeaway: Field 56 names the intermediary. Field 55 names the reimbursement bank. Swap them and the funds go astray.

title: EUR 90,000 debited, and the customer demanded proof that never came
explain:
EUR 90,000 was debited on an MT103 instruction.
The customer asked for proof of the debit.
No MT900 ever arrived, and the customer assumed the payment had failed.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank debits the account on the MT103
→ No MT900 confirmation sent
→ Customer sees the debit but no proof
→ Customer assumes the payment failed

The assumption was:
"Every debit is confirmed with an MT900."
Whether one is sent depends on the agreement between the two banks.

Why?

When a bank debits an account on the instruction of an MT103, it can confirm the debit with an MT900, a confirmation of debit. The MT900 is a separate message, not part of the MT103 itself, and a payment can therefore settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged.

A payment can settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged.

What proves this payment settled, with or without an MT900?

BA Takeaway

Prove settlement from the account entries and the MT103, not from the presence of an MT900. Tell the customer upfront whether an MT900 is part of the agreement, so silence is not read as failure.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Debit posted
→ MT103 instruction
→ MT900 agreement
→ Settlement proven from the entries

The real requirement isn't "Was an MT900 sent?"

It's "What evidence proves this payment settled, with or without an MT900?"

Have you ever had a customer read silence as a failed payment?
takeaway: A payment can settle correctly without any MT900 being exchanged.

title: USD 175,000 with no SSI on file, and no one knew where to send it
explain:
USD 175,000 had to be paid to a beneficiary bank.
The sending bank had no standing settlement instruction on file for that bank.
No one knew which correspondent to send the funds to, and the payment waited.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment due to the beneficiary bank
→ No SSI on file for that bank in USD
→ Correspondent unknown
→ Payment held while the route is found

The assumption was:
"The payment engine will know where to send it."
Without an SSI, the engine has nothing to build the payment from.

Why?

Banks tell each other how to send them funds in each currency through standing settlement instructions, exchanged as MT670 and MT671 messages and stored in payment engine databases. An SSI names the correspondent of the receiver and any intermediaries on the route, so the sending bank can build the MT103 and the cover from the database instead of asking every time.

Without an SSI, the sender must find the correspondent before the payment can move.

What proves we know the receiver's correspondent for this currency?

BA Takeaway

Keep SSIs current in the payment engine database. When one is missing, find the correspondent through SWIFT services or by asking the receiver directly, and never guess the route.

Keep these controls separate:

→ SSI on file
→ Correspondent named
→ Intermediaries on the route
→ Payment built from the SSI

The real requirement isn't "Can we send this payment?"

It's "What evidence proves we know the receiver's correspondent for this currency?"

Have you ever held a payment because no SSI was on file?
takeaway: Without an SSI, the sender must find the correspondent before the payment can move.

agenda: Work through this case: USD 175,000 with no SSI on file, and no one knew where to send it. USD 175,000 had to be paid to a beneficiary bank. The sending bank had no standing settlement instruction on file for that bank. No one knew which correspondent to send the funds to, and the payment waited. One thing to remember: Without an SSI, the sender must find the correspondent before the payment can move.

title: EUR 80,000 sent to the wrong bank because field 57a was read the same way twice
explain:
EUR 80,000 was sent in a cover payment.
The team read field 57a the way it works in a serial MT103.
The funds went to the beneficiary bank's correspondent instead of the beneficiary bank.

Here's how that happens:

→ Serial MT103 read first, field 57a noted
→ MT202 COV read the same way
→ Field 57a points at a different bank in each leg
→ Funds sent to the wrong bank

The assumption was:
"Field 57a always means the same bank."
The same field number points at a different bank in each leg.

Why?

In a serial MT103, field 57a names the bank that holds the beneficiary's account, and field 56 names the intermediary that forwards the payment to it. In an MT202 COV the roles shift: field 58a names the beneficiary bank, while field 57a names the correspondent bank of the beneficiary bank.

The same field number points at a different bank in each leg.

What proves we read field 57a for the leg we are actually in?

BA Takeaway

Read field 57a per message: in a serial MT103 it is the bank holding the beneficiary's account, in an MT202 COV it is the beneficiary bank's correspondent. Check field 58a for the beneficiary bank on the cover leg.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 57a in the MT103
→ Field 57a in the MT202 COV
→ Field 58a in the MT202 COV
→ Field 56 in the MT103

The real requirement isn't "Which bank does field 57a name?"

It's "What evidence proves we read field 57a for the leg we are actually in?"

Have you ever sent funds to the wrong bank by reading a field the same way twice?
takeaway: The same field number points at a different bank in each leg.
